claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Naglik et al., 2019.

claims.claim: Cellular damage caused by CL activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators.
claims.source: The resulting cellular damage activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators (Naglik et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2018b), which participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Naglik et al., 2019 and Richardson et al., 2018b.

claims.claim: Pro-inflammatory mediators released in response to CL participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
claims.source: The resulting cellular damage activates a signaling cascade that triggers the release of pro-inflammatory mediators (Naglik et al., 2019; Richardson et al., 2018b), which participate in the immune response to C. albicans infection.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the cited literature and established immunological knowledge.

claims.claim: CL attacks the membrane of mononuclear phagocytes.
claims.source: Furthermore, CL plays a second pathogenic role, as it also attacks the membrane of mononuclear phagocytes which would otherwise fight the fungal infection (Kasper et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kasper et al., 2018.

claims.claim: CL is necessary for infection by C. albicans.
claims.source: CL is necessary for infection by C. albicans (Liu et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Liu et al., 2021.

claims.claim: Pharmacological inhibition of CL activity is a promising avenue to fight infection of C. albicans.
claims.source: Therefore, pharmacological inhibition of CL activity is a promising avenue to fight infection of this human pathogen.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference based on the necessity of CL for infection.

claims.claim: The development of drugs to counter the action of CL is hampered by the lack of understanding of how this peptide damages membranes.
claims.source: However, the development of drugs to counter the action of CL is hampered by the lack of understanding of how this peptide damages membranes.
claims.evidence: This is a logical statement about the relationship between mechanistic understanding and drug development.

claims.claim: CL self-assembles in solution.
claims.source: This result suggests that CL self-assembles in solution, and we hypothesized that this event might be related to its ability to damage cellular membranes.
claims.evidence: This is supported by SDS-PAGE data showing oligomeric bands in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: IM-MS analysis of CL revealed several oligomeric species.
claims.source: IM-MS analysis of CL revealed several oligomeric species (Figure 1B).
claims.evidence: This is directly supported by the IM-MS data shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The mass spectral peak at m/z 3311 corresponds to a nominal oligomer-to-charge ratio (n/z) of 1/1.
claims.source: The mass spectral peak at m/z 3311, which corresponds to a nominal oligomer-to-charge ratio (n/z) of 1/1, was notable due to its high intensity when compared to the surrounding oligomers.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the IM-MS data in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: The longest arrival time feature in the ATD corresponds to an 8-mer with z = +8.
claims.source: We conservatively assigned the longest arrival time feature (salmon) as an 8-mer with z = +8.
claims.evidence: This assignment is based on analysis of isotopic spacing and drift time data shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The fastest arrival time species is proposed to be a large oligomer resulting from the self-assembly of the 8-mer.
claims.source: Since a species with a high charge will travel faster than one with a lower charge, the fastest arrival time species (green) is proposed to be a large oligomer resulting from the self-assembly of the 8-mer.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the IM-MS data and principles of ion mobility.

claims.claim: CL adopts helical structure in solution.
claims.source: Given that CL adopts helical structure in solution (Moyes et al., 2016), we built an atomistic model of the 8-mer by aligning CL's sequence into the eight-helix coiled coil formed by CC-Type2-II (PDB ID 6G67).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Moyes et al., 2016.

claims.claim: The theoretical collisional cross-section of the CL 8-mer model (2500 Å2) agrees with the experimental value of 2567 Å2.
claims.source: After the resulting structure was energy minimized (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), the theoretical collisional cross-section of the model, 2500 Å2, agreed with the experimental value of 2567 Å2.
claims.evidence: This comparison between theoretical and experimental values supports the validity of the 8-mer model.

claims.claim: Analytical ultracentrifugation data identifies populations of increasingly larger CL oligomers.
claims.source: Analytical ultracentrifugation data identifies populations of increasingly larger CL oligomers.
claims.evidence: This is directly shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Mass photometry data of CL shows oligomeric species with masses corresponding to 2, 3, 4, 8, 13, and 22 CL 8-mers.
claims.source: Data distribution was best fit with six Gaussian populations (shown as blue lines, and summary fit is the black line). The mass of the peaks agree with the expected mass for 2, 3, 4, 8, 13, and 22 CL 8-mers (similar to a Fibonacci sequence).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of the mass photometry data shown in Figure 1E.

claims.claim: CL does not form amorphous aggregates, but instead assembles into linear structures.
claims.source: We first performed negative-stain transmission electron microscopy (TEM), and observed that CL does not form amorphous aggregates, but instead assembles into linear structures (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the TEM data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: TEM data revealed a basic structural unit that grows in a step-wise fashion into polymers.
claims.source: The TEM data revealed a basic structural unit, which seemed to grow in a step-wise fashion into polymers (Figure 2A, side panels).
claims.evidence: This is observed in the TEM images shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: Longer CL polymers curve and in some cases close in on themselves, forming a loop with diameter ≥10 nm.
claims.source: The longer polymers curved, and in some cases closed in on themselves, forming a loop with diameter ≥10 nm.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the TEM data shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: AFM images of CL adsorbed onto mica in buffer confirmed that CL polymerizes and can form loops.
claims.source: AFM images of CL adsorbed onto mica in buffer (Figure 2B) agreed with the TEM results and confirmed that CL polymerizes and can form loops.
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in the AFM data shown in Figure 2B.

claims.claim: The bending stiffness of CL polymers, calculated from persistence length analysis, is Lp = 9 nm±2 nm.
claims.source: The bending stiffness of CL polymers was calculated from AFM images through persistence length, Lp, analysis (Lp = 9 nm±2 nm, N=100, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is calculated from AFM data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The bending stiffness of linear CL polymers is significantly lower than other biological polymers, like actin fibers.
claims.source: The bending stiffness of linear CL polymers is significantly lower than other biological polymers, like actin fibers (Gittes et al., 1993), explaining the ability of CL polymers to close into loops.
claims.evidence: This comparison is made with cited literature on actin fibers.

claims.claim: The volume histogram of CL features from AFM has a sharp peak and a long tail.
claims.source: Examination of AFM images containing thousands of particles yielded a volume distribution with a sharp peak and a long tail (Figure 2C), which resembles the distribution observed in the MP data (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the AFM volume histogram in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The AFM volume histogram resembles the distribution observed in the MP data.
claims.source: Examination of AFM images containing thousands of particles yielded a volume distribution with a sharp peak and a long tail (Figure 2C), which resembles the distribution observed in the MP data (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This comparison between AFM and MP data supports the robustness of the observations.

claims.claim: The AFM volume histogram was deconvolved by fitting Gaussian distributions, revealing a primary peak and several larger sub-populations.
claims.source: The AFM volume histogram was deconvolved by fitting Gaussian distributions, revealing a primary peak and several larger sub-populations of larger volumes (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the analysis of Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The volume increased in approximately constant steps between the populations.
claims.source: The volume increased in approximately constant steps between the populations (see side panels of Figure 2B), confirming that a basic intermediate oligomer grew first by dimerization, followed by sequential addition to further increase linear polymer length.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the AFM data and volume analysis shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claims.claim: The height histogram of individual CL particles from AFM yielded two peaks, with heights of 3.2±0.4 nm and 4.6±0.5 nm.
claims.source: We measured the height of the individual particles observed by AFM, and the resulting histogram (Figure 2D) yielded two peaks, with heights of 3.2±0.4 nm and 4.6±0.5 nm.
claims.evidence: This is directly measured from AFM data shown in Figure 2D.

claims.claim: The bimodal height distribution indicates two orientations (vertical and horizontal) of the basic structural unit.
claims.source: We reasoned that the bimodal height distribution could indicate two orientations (vertical and horizontal) of the basic structural unit that serves as an intermediate oligomer (Figure 2B inset, labeled '1'), which is probably the CL 8-mer identified by IM-MS (Figure 1B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the AFM height data and comparison with the 8-mer model.

claims.claim: Simulated AFM images of the CL 8-mer in horizontal or vertical orientations yielded heights of 3.3 nm and 4.8 nm.
claims.source: We tested this possibility by using the CL 8-mer model (Figure 1—figure supplement 1) to generate simulated AFM images through morphological dilation of the estimated tip geometry for the 8-mer, either on its horizontal or vertical orientations (Figure 2D, insets). We found good agreement between the simulation [heights of 3.3 nm and 4.8 nm] and the two experimental peaks shown in Figure 2D.
claims.evidence: This is based on AFM simulations compared to experimental data.

claims.claim: The volume of the modeled 8-mer in the horizontal orientation agrees with the value of the basic AFM structural unit.
claims.source: Interestingly, the volume of the modeled 8-mer in the horizontal orientation additionally agrees within uncertainty with the value of the basic AFM structural unit (Figure 2C inset).
claims.evidence: This comparison between model and experimental data supports the 8-mer hypothesis.

claims.claim: CL assembles into an 8-mer in solution that acts as an intermediate step in the self-assembly process.
claims.source: Taken together, these results support the notion that CL assembles into an 8-mer in solution that acts as an intermediate step in the self-assembly process.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of evidence including IM-MS, AFM, and modeling.

claims.claim: Polymer growth of CL 8-mers in the horizontal orientation can occur by side-by-side or head-to-toe addition.
claims.source: Polymer growth of CL 8-mers in the horizontal orientation (lying flat on a surface) can occur by addition of a second 8-mer in two fundamental modes, side-by-side or head-to-toe.
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference about possible assembly modes.

claims.claim: Modeling of head-to-toe assembly of two, three, and four 8-mers shows agreement between simulated and experimental AFM volumes.
claims.source: When we modeled the latter arrangement for the assembly of two, three, and four head-to-toe 8-mers (Figure 2C, inset), we found agreement between the simulated and experimental AFM volumes (Figure 2C, inset; Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This comparison between simulations and experimental data supports the head-to-toe assembly model.

claims.claim: A CL polymer is formed when a basic subunit is aligned in the longest dimension and grows by sequential head-to-toe addition of additional subunits.
claims.source: Taken together, the data indicate that a CL polymer is formed when a basic subunit, which our results suggest is an 8-mer, is aligned in the longest dimension, and grows by sequential head-to-toe addition of additional subunits.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on AFM volume analysis and modeling.

claims.claim: CL forms membrane pores.
claims.source: It has been proposed that CL forms membrane pores (Moyes et al., 2016), but such structures have never been observed.
claims.evidence: This is supported by AFM imaging showing pore-like depressions in lipid bilayers in the presence of CL.

claims.claim: In the presence of CL, DOPC bilayers exhibited punctate depressions commonly associated with pores.
claims.source: We performed AFM imaging on supported lipid bilayers made of DOPC (1,2-dioleoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine) to gain insights into how CL causes membrane disruption. We observed that in the presence of CL, bilayers indeed exhibited punctate depressions commonly associated with pores (Figure 3A).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in AFM images shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (unrimmed) and complex pores surrounded by a rim (rimmed).
claims.source: The CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (Figure 3A), and complex pores surrounded by a rim of discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is observed in AFM images shown in Figures 3A and 3B.

claims.claim: Rimmed pores are surrounded by discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface.
claims.source: The CL pores fell into two broad categories: simple depressions (Figure 3A), and complex pores surrounded by a rim of discrete protrusions of an approximate height of 0.3 nm above the bilayer surface (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is measured from AFM data shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer.
claims.source: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
claims.evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
claims.source: Both types of pores were free to diffuse in the bilayer (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), indicating that CL is not immobilized by interactions with the mica surface.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation of pore diffusion.

claims.claim: Rimmed pores generally have a smaller area than unrimmed pores.
claims.source: Rimmed pores generally have a smaller area than unrimmed pores (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2.
claims.source: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2 (Figure 3C, gray), while the rimmed pores have a narrower distribution, and an area peak at 26 nm2 (Figure 3C, black).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Rimmed pores have a narrower area distribution, with an area peak at 26 nm2.
claims.source: Unrimmed pores have a broad area distribution, with the main population at 41 nm2 (Figure 3C, gray), while the rimmed pores have a narrower distribution, and an area peak at 26 nm2 (Figure 3C, black).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the area histogram in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: Unrimmed pores show dynamic behavior, with large variations over time.
claims.source: A representative unrimmed pore (Figure 3D, top row) shows dynamic behavior, with large variations over time. The pore depth visibly varies, flickering between deep and shallow states.
claims.evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: Rimmed pores appear deeper and are more stable than unrimmed pores.
claims.source: On the other hand, the rimmed pore (Figure 3D, bottom row) appears deeper, and is more stable, as shown by the constant profile over time (Figure 3E).
claims.evidence: This is observed in time-series AFM imaging shown in Figure 3D and 3E.

claims.claim: The presence of the rim endows the pore with increased stability.
claims.source: While the two types of pores are likely to cause membrane permeabilization, we propose that the presence of the rim endows the pore with increased stability, which could potentially be a mechanism to afford CL pores with enhanced membrane damaging capabilities.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the observation that rimmed pores are more stable over time.

claims.claim: There are strong similarities between the shape and size of the loops that CL forms in the absence of membrane and the unrimmed membrane pores.
claims.source: We noticed that there were strong similarities between the shape and size of the loops that CL forms in the absence of membrane and the unrimmed membrane pores (Figure 3C, compare blue and gray lines).
claims.evidence: This is observed by comparing the area distributions in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: CL loops can insert into membranes and become unrimmed pores.
claims.source: This agreement led us to hypothesize that CL loops could insert into membranes and become unrimmed pores.
claims.evidence: This hypothesis is supported by observations of loops and pores after lipid dissociation, shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Loops were observed where pores were previously present after lipid dissociation.
claims.source: Upon imaging the exact same area again, we observed features similar to the CL polymers and loops detected in the absence of lipid bilayers. Indeed, loops, often inter-connected, were observed where pores were previously present (see blue arrows).
claims.evidence: This is directly observed in AFM images shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption.
claims.source: Linear features similar to the CL polymers observed for solution samples were also present, which had been previously obscured by the presence of a bilayer. This observation indicates that linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption, but when they close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: When linear polymers close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
claims.source: This observation indicates that linear polymers can insert into membranes without causing membrane disruption, but when they close into a loop they form an unrimmed membrane pore.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from AFM observations shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Detergent (DβM) was used to forcibly remove lipid bilayers.
claims.source: In order to replicate these spontaneous events in a deterministic manner, we used the mild detergent dodecyl beta-D-maltoside (DβM) to remove the lipid bilayer (Milhiet et al., 2006; Rinia et al., 2001).
claims.evidence: This is a methodological approach supported by citations.

claims.claim: DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support.
claims.source: Control experiments showed that DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support, but did not dissociate the CL polymers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1);
claims.evidence: This is shown in control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: DβM did not dissociate the CL polymers.
claims.source: Control experiments showed that DβM efficiently removed DOPC molecules from the mica support, but did not dissociate the CL polymers (Figure 4—figure supplement 1);
claims.evidence: This is shown in control experiments in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Detergent treatment might reduce the fraction of polymers that close into a loop.
claims.source: however, our data suggest that detergent treatment might reduce the fraction of polymers that close into a loop (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is suggested by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The vertical 8-mer orientation is favored in the presence of lipid membranes.
claims.source: However, the increase in taller features could also be an indication that the vertical 8-mer orientation (Figure 2D) is favored in the presence of lipid membranes.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the height histogram comparison in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: Loops found in solution assemble in a head-to-toe fashion.
claims.source: Comparison between the experimental inner areas and the models (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1) suggest that the loops found in solution, similar to the linear polymers, assemble into a head-to-toe fashion.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from comparison between experimental data and models shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The average loop is composed of six head-to-toe 8-mers, for a mass of 159 kDa.
claims.source: The average loop would be composed of six head-to-toe 8-mers, for a mass (159 kDa) that corresponds with the start of the tail in the MP distribution (Figure 1E).
claims.evidence: This is inferred from modeling and comparison with mass photometry data.

claims.claim: CL forms an α-helical structure in solution.
claims.source: Figure 5B shows that CL forms, as expected (Moyes et al., 2016), an α-helical structure in solution, as evidenced by the spectral minima at 208 and 222 nm.
claims.evidence: This is shown by circular dichroism data in Figure 5B and supported by citation.

claims.claim: The presence of lipid vesicles promotes modest additional helix formation in CL.
claims.source: We also observed that the presence of lipid vesicles promotes modest additional helix formation, possibly by growth of the α-helix and its ends.
claims.evidence: This is observed in the CD data shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The OCD data of CL indicate that the predominant orientation of helices in membranes is transmembrane.
claims.source: The OCD data of CL displayed low intensity, and a minimum at ~225 nm and a maximum at ~195 nm, similarly to the expected result for TM helices (Alves et al., 2018; Stefanski et al., 2021). The OCD spectrum therefore indicates that the predominant orientation of helices in CL in membranes was inserted across the membrane, in a TM orientation.
claims.evidence: This is shown by OCD data in Figure 5C and comparison with expected spectra for TM helices.

claims.claim: The OCD spectrum supports the presence of a population of α-helices oriented along the plane of the membrane.
claims.source: However, the presence of a depression at ~210 nm agrees with the presence of a population of α-helices oriented along the plane of the membrane, like those expected for the unrimmed pore.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the OCD spectrum shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The OCD result supports the presence of a combination of rimmed and unrimmed CL pores with the respective helical orientations predicted by the AFM modeling.
claims.source: Therefore, the OCD result supports the presence of a combination of rimmed and unrimmed CL pores with the respective helical orientations predicted by the AFM modeling.
claims.evidence: This conclusion integrates OCD data with AFM modeling results.

claims.claim: A head-to-toe assembly of a parallel helical bundle implies interaction between the N-terminal helical ends of an 8-mer with the C-termini of the adjacent subunit.
claims.source: A head-to-toe assembly of a parallel helical bundle implies interaction between the N-terminal (Nt) helical ends of an 8-mer with the C-termini of the adjacent subunit (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: This is a logical inference from the head-to-toe assembly model.

claims.claim: The 8-mer model predicts that the N-terminus is slightly kinked at residue G4.
claims.source: Our 8-mer model predicts that the Nt is slightly kinked at residue G4 (Figure 6A).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the model structure in Figure 6A.

claims.claim: Glycine residues confer flexibility to α-helices.
claims.source: Since glycine residues confer flexibility to α-helices (Choy et al., 2003), we reasoned that the mutation of residue G4 (Figure 6A) might affect CL self-assembly.
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to Choy et al., 2003.

claims.claim: G4W formed few large assemblies in solution.
claims.source: We first tested the ability of the resulting G4W CL variant to polymerize in solution using MP, and observed that G4W formed few large assemblies (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the mass photometry data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The I9A variant self-assembles efficiently in solution.
claims.source: The MP results show that the I9A variant, on the other hand, self-assembles efficiently in solution (Figure 6B).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the mass photometry data in Figure 6B.

claims.claim: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features compared to WT.
claims.source: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features, while G4W does not form polymers; scale bar = 100 nm.
claims.evidence: This is shown in AFM images in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: G4W does not form polymers.
claims.source: The I9A variant exhibits increased loop features, while G4W does not form polymers; scale bar = 100 nm.
claims.evidence: This is shown in AFM images in Figure 6C.

claims.claim: I9A forms membrane pores.
claims.source: I9A CL forms membrane pores, while pores were not observed for G4W; scale bars = 100 nm for full images, 10 nm for inset.
claims.evidence: This is shown in AFM images of membranes in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: Pores were not observed for G4W.
claims.source: I9A CL forms membrane pores, while pores were not observed for G4W; scale bars = 100 nm for full images, 10 nm for inset.
claims.evidence: This is shown in AFM images of membranes in Figure 6F.

claims.claim: G4W did not induce membrane disruption in the liposome dye release assay.
claims.source: Figure 6G shows the kinetics of membrane disruption caused by the addition of WT and the two CL variants. We observed that G4W did not induce membrane disruption, in agreement with the lack of membrane pores observed by AFM.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes in the liposome dye release assay.
claims.source: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes, but I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity, as expected from the high loop formation probability (Figure 6E) and the presence of larger membrane pores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity.
claims.source: WT CL efficiently disrupted membranes, but I9A was the most efficacious at disrupting membrane integrity, as expected from the high loop formation probability (Figure 6E) and the presence of larger membrane pores (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the liposome dye release assay in Figure 6G.

claims.claim: G4W showed reduced helical structure in solution and in the presence of POPC liposomes.
claims.source: CD revealed that G4W showed reduced helical structure in solution and in the presence of POPC liposomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is shown in CD data in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: I9A displayed higher levels of oligomeric intermediates on SDS-PAGE.
claims.source: When we performed SDS-PAGE of the variants, we observed that I9A displayed higher levels of oligomeric intermediates (Figure 6H).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the SDS-PAGE gel in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: The higher tendency of I9A to polymerize is due to its enhanced oligomerization ability.
claims.source: This result suggests that the higher tendency of I9A to polymerize is due to its enhanced oligomerization ability.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the SDS-PAGE data showing higher oligomer levels for I9A.

claims.claim: G4W displayed similar levels of oligomers as WT on SDS-PAGE.
claims.source: G4W, on the other hand, displayed similar levels of oligomers as WT.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the SDS-PAGE gel in Figure 6H.

claims.claim: A tryptophan at the N-terminus might impair the ability of two oligomers to bind.
claims.source: We therefore speculate that a W present at the Nt might impair the ability of two oligomers to bind.
claims.evidence: This is speculation based on the G4W mutation data.

claims.claim: Formation of polymers in solution is a necessary step for the formation of membrane pores.
claims.source: The results of the loss-of-function G4W variant revealed that formation of polymers in solution is a necessary step for the formation of membrane pores.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the G4W data showing no polymerization and no pore formation.

claims.claim: CL pores damage the plasma membrane of epithelial cells.
claims.source: CL pores damage the plasma membrane of epithelial cells.
claims.evidence: This is supported by established knowledge and the cellular assay data.

claims.claim: CL attack triggers the activation of danger response signaling, which induces phosphorylation of MAPK phosphatase 1 (MKP1) and subsequent overexpression of the transcription factor c-Fos.
claims.source: This attack triggers the activation of danger response signaling, which induces phosphorylation of MAPK phosphatase 1 (MKP1) and subsequent overexpression of the transcription factor c-Fos (Richardson et al., 2018b; Richardson et al., 2018a).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to Richardson et al., 2018a and 2018b.

claims.claim: WT CL induced robust increases in c-Fos (threefold) levels and phosphorylation of MKP1 (5-fold) in TR146 cells.
claims.source: When we treated the oral epithelial cell line TR146 with WT CL, we observed robust increases in c-Fos (threefold) levels and phosphorylation of MKP1 (5-fold) (Figure 7), as expected (Moyes et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: The I9A variant induced strong MKP1 phosphorylation and significantly higher c-Fos expression than WT.
claims.source: The I9A variant also induced strong MKP1 phosphorylation, but significantly higher c-Fos expression.
claims.evidence: This is shown in the Western blot data in Figure 7.

claims.claim: Mutations that alter polymerization impact epithelial cell damage response signaling.
claims.source: Our data therefore indicate that mutations that alter polymerization impact epithelial cell damage response signaling.
claims.evidence: This conclusion is based on the cellular assay data for the variants.

claims.claim: Polymerization of CL in solution is a major factor defining C. albicans infection.
claims.source: Taken together, these results suggest that polymerization of CL in solution is a major factor defining C. albicans infection.
claims.evidence: This conclusion integrates biophysical and cellular data.

claims.claim: Pore-forming toxins (PFTs) are typically released as soluble monomers that later bind to the target lipid bilayer.
claims.source: PFTs are typically released as soluble monomers that later bind to the target lipid bilayer.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge about PFT mechanisms.

claims.claim: After membrane binding, PFT monomers find each other and oligomerize.
claims.source: After membrane binding, PFT monomers find each other and oligomerize (Leung et al., 2014; Verma et al., 2021), often forming membrane-anchored pre-pores that later transition into the mature pores that permeabilize membranes (Mondal and Chattopadhyay, 2020; De Schutter et al., 2021).
claims.evidence: This statement is supported by citations to multiple studies on PFT mechanisms.

claims.claim: CL follows a different molecular mechanism for pore formation than typical PFTs.
claims.source: Here, we show that CL follows a different molecular mechanism for pore formation.
claims.evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by all the experimental data.

claims.claim: CL forms both linear and closed loop polymers before binding to the membrane.
claims.source: Multiple lines of evidence indicate that CL forms both linear and closed loop polymers before binding to the membrane (Figure 8).
claims.evidence: This is supported by TEM, AFM, and other biophysical data.

claims.claim: Closed loop CL polymers insert into lipid bilayers to cause membrane damage without any observable conformational change.
claims.source: Further, acting as soluble pre-pores, closed loop CL polymers insert into lipid bilayers to cause membrane damage without any observable conformational change.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from AFM data showing similar structures for loops in solution and unrimmed pores in membranes.

claims.claim: CL assembles into intermediate size membrane pores, of diameter ≤80 Å.
claims.source: AFM imaging revealed that CL (3.3 kDa) assembles into intermediate size membrane pores, of diameter ≤80 Å, deduced from area distribution peaks <50 nm2 (Figures 5A and 3C) and assuming circularity, which matched many of the pores observed.
claims.evidence: This is calculated from AFM area measurements.

results.result: CL assembles into polymers in solution with an 8-mer as the basic structural unit. Multiple biophysical techniques (SDS-PAGE, IM-MS, analytical ultracentrifugation, mass photometry, TEM, AFM) demonstrate that CL forms oligomers and larger assemblies in solution, with evidence supporting an 8-mer as the fundamental building block that polymerizes into linear structures and loops.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C31-C54 are supported by convergent evidence from multiple independent techniques (IM-MS, mass photometry, analytical ultracentrifugation, TEM, AFM). The 8-mer assignment is based on collisional cross-section agreement between experimental (2567 Ų) and theoretical (2500 Ų) values (C37), AFM height and volume analysis (C50-C53), and modeling. The authors acknowledge uncertainty in the precise stoichiometry (C130-C131), which is appropriate given the technical challenges.

results.result: CL polymers grow by sequential head-to-toe addition of 8-mer subunits. AFM volume analysis shows stepwise increases consistent with sequential addition of subunits (C49), and modeling of head-to-toe assemblies agrees with experimental volumes (C56). Loops in solution are proposed to contain approximately six head-to-toe 8-mers (C81).
results.evaluation: Claims C4-C5, C55-C57, C80-C81 are supported by AFM volume analysis showing stepwise growth (C49) and agreement between simulated and experimental volumes for head-to-toe arrangements (C56). The head-to-toe model is further validated by mutational analysis (G4W affecting N-terminus) and is consistent across multiple lines of evidence.

results.result: CL forms two distinct types of membrane pores: unrimmed pores (simple depressions) and rimmed pores (surrounded by discrete protrusions ~0.3 nm above the bilayer). AFM imaging reveals that unrimmed pores are dynamic and have a broad area distribution (41 nm²), while rimmed pores are more stable with a narrower distribution (26 nm²). Both pore types diffuse freely in the bilayer.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C69 and C11 are well-supported by AFM imaging data showing two morphologically distinct pore types with different area distributions, stability profiles, and dynamic behavior. Time-series AFM imaging (C67-C68) provides direct evidence for the differential stability. The observation that both pore types diffuse (C62) rules out artifacts from surface interactions.

results.result: CL loops formed in solution spontaneously insert into membranes to become unrimmed pores. The similarity in size and shape between solution loops and unrimmed pores (C70), combined with direct observation of loops at sites where pores existed after lipid dissociation (C72), supports this mechanism. Detergent removal experiments confirm that loops remain after lipid is removed (C76-C77).
results.evaluation: Claims C6, C70-C77, C115 are supported by multiple lines of evidence: (1) area distribution similarity between loops and unrimmed pores (C70), (2) direct AFM observation of loops at former pore sites after spontaneous lipid dissociation (C72), and (3) controlled detergent removal experiments (C75-C77). The inference that loops become pores is well-justified by the convergent data.

results.result: Rimmed pores form through a maturation mechanism involving 90-degree rotation of 8-mer subunits from head-to-toe to side-by-side orientation. OCD data indicate predominant transmembrane helix orientation consistent with rimmed pores, with a population of membrane-parallel helices consistent with unrimmed pores (C84-C86). The rim height (~0.3 nm) corresponds to helix ends protruding from the bilayer (C121).
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C13, C79, C84-C86, C121-C123, C135-C137 propose a maturation mechanism based on modeling and OCD data. While the OCD data support mixed helix orientations (C84-C86) and AFM shows rimmed pores are more stable (C68), the 90-degree rotation mechanism is largely inferred from modeling rather than directly observed. The progressive maturation (C122) is suggested but not rigorously quantified. Additional structural data would strengthen this conclusion.

results.result: The G4W mutation prevents CL polymerization in solution and abolishes pore formation and cellular toxicity. Mass photometry and AFM show G4W forms few large assemblies (C90, C93), no membrane pores are observed by AFM (C95), liposome dye release assays show no membrane disruption (C96), and epithelial cells show no danger response activation (C9). This demonstrates that polymerization in solution is necessary for membrane damage.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C10, C90, C93, C95-C96, C102, C104 are strongly supported by convergent loss-of-function data across multiple assays (mass photometry, AFM, liposome leakage, Western blot). The G4W mutation provides a critical test of the polymerization-dependent mechanism. The conclusion that polymerization is necessary for membrane damage (C10, C104) is well-justified by the complete loss of function across all assays.

results.result: The I9A variant shows enhanced polymerization, increased loop formation, larger membrane pores, and greater membrane disruption compared to wild-type CL. Mass photometry shows efficient self-assembly (C91), AFM reveals increased loop features (C92) and larger pores (C133-C134), liposome assays show enhanced membrane disruption (C98), and cellular assays show significantly higher c-Fos expression (C108).
results.evaluation: Claims C91-C92, C94, C97-C98, C100-C101, C108, C133-C134 are supported by consistent gain-of-function data across biophysical and cellular assays. The correlation between increased loop formation in solution (C92) and larger pores in membranes (C133-C134) provides strong support for the loop-to-pore mechanism. SDS-PAGE data showing higher oligomer levels (C100-C101) provides a mechanistic explanation.

results.result: CL forms α-helical structure in solution, with modest additional helix formation in the presence of lipid vesicles. CD spectroscopy shows characteristic α-helix minima at 208 and 222 nm (C82). The G4W variant shows reduced helical structure in both solution and lipid environments (C99).
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83, C99 are supported by CD spectroscopy data. The α-helical structure in solution (C82) is consistent with prior literature (Moyes et al., 2016) and the 8-mer coiled-coil model. The reduced helicity of G4W (C99) may contribute to its loss of function, though the relative importance of structural versus assembly defects is unclear.

results.result: CL-induced membrane damage activates danger response signaling in epithelial cells, with mutations affecting polymerization impacting cellular responses. Wild-type CL induces robust c-Fos expression (3-fold) and MKP1 phosphorylation (5-fold) in TR146 cells (C107), while mutations that alter polymerization (I9A, G4W) show corresponding changes in cellular signaling (C109).
results.evaluation: Claims C105-C107, C109-C110 are supported by Western blot data showing differential activation of danger response markers (c-Fos, pMKP1) by CL variants. The correlation between polymerization ability and cellular response (C109-C110) is consistent across the three variants tested, though the sample size (N=4) is modest. The conclusion that polymerization is a major factor in infection (C110) is well-supported.

results.result: CL uses a novel pore formation mechanism distinct from typical pore-forming toxins, involving pre-assembly of loops in solution that insert into membranes. This represents a previously unknown mechanism for membrane pore formation and identifies CL polymerization as a therapeutic target.
results.evaluation: Claims C14, C113-C114, C132 represent the main conclusions of the study, supported by the totality of evidence showing: (1) polymerization in solution (multiple techniques), (2) loop formation before membrane binding (AFM), (3) loop insertion to form pores (detergent removal, area similarity), and (4) necessity of polymerization for function (G4W mutation). The novelty claim is justified by comparison with known PFT mechanisms (C111-C112).

results.result: CL forms intermediate-sized membrane pores (~80 Å diameter) that are smaller than pores formed by gasdermin-D, suilysin, and perfringolysin O, but likely larger than α-hemolysin pores. Unrimmed CL pores are topographically similar to melittin-induced structures, while rimmed pores are more stable on AFM imaging timescales.
results.evaluation: Claims C116-C120 are supported by AFM area measurements and comparisons with literature values for other pore-forming proteins. The pore size calculation from area distributions (C116) is reasonable assuming circularity. The comparison with melittin (C119) is appropriate given the similar topography, though functional similarities are not established.

results.result: Linear CL polymers can insert into membranes without causing visible membrane disruption, but become pores when they close into loops. This is inferred from AFM observations after lipid removal showing linear features that were previously obscured by the bilayer.
results.evaluation: Claims C126 and C73 are supported by AFM observations after spontaneous or detergent-induced lipid dissociation showing linear polymers that were not visible when the bilayer was intact. This suggests linear polymers insert but don't disrupt the bilayer surface significantly. The inference is reasonable but relies on the assumption that the structures observed after lipid removal reflect the pre-removal state.

results.result: The stability difference between unrimmed and rimmed pores may relate to lysine residue positioning. In unrimmed pores, lysine side chains would contact lipids (meta-stable), while in rimmed pores they would be solvent-exposed (more stable).
results.evaluation: Claims C124-C125 are speculative proposals about the energetic basis for pore maturation. While the reasoning about charged residue positioning is plausible, there is no direct experimental evidence (e.g., mutagenesis of lysine residues, molecular dynamics simulations) to support this specific mechanism. The speculation is reasonable but requires validation.

results.result: The pre-assembly mechanism may provide an infectivity advantage for C. albicans and represents a therapeutic opportunity. Molecules that prevent CL polymerization or loop formation could serve as therapeutics against C. albicans infection.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C129 are speculative proposals about biological significance and therapeutic potential. While the logic is sound (faster membrane damage, druggable target in solution), there is no experimental evidence that the pre-assembly mechanism actually provides an advantage in vivo, nor any demonstration of inhibitor molecules. These are reasonable hypotheses for future work but are not supported by data in this study.

results.result: Background claims about C. albicans pathogenesis and the role of candidalysin. These include statements about C. albicans as a serious fungal pathogen, its role in invasive candidiasis, the discovery and function of candidalysin as a virulence factor, and the rationale for studying its mechanism of action.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C2, C15-C30 are background statements supported by established literature (multiple citations to Brown et al., Kullberg and Arendrup, Moyes et al., Naglik et al., Richardson et al., Kasper et al., Liu et al.). These provide appropriate context for the study and are well-documented in the literature. The logical inference about drug development (C29-C30) is reasonable.

results.result: Speculative mechanistic proposals about detergent effects on loop formation and the role of tryptophan at the N-terminus in impairing oligomer binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C78 and C103 are acknowledged as speculative by the authors. C78 suggests detergent might reduce loop formation based on limited data. C103 proposes a mechanism for G4W loss of function but lacks direct evidence (e.g., binding assays, structural data). These are reasonable hypotheses but require experimental validation.

results.result: Rationale for the G4W mutation based on the 8-mer model predicting a kink at G4 and the known flexibility conferred by glycine residues in α-helices.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C89 provide the structural rationale for testing the G4W mutation. The model prediction of a kink at G4 (C88) is shown in Figure 6A, and the role of glycine in helix flexibility (C89) is supported by citation to Choy et al., 2003. This represents sound experimental design based on structural modeling.

results.result: Background on typical pore-forming toxin mechanisms, stating that PFTs are usually released as monomers that bind membranes and then oligomerize, often forming pre-pores before mature pores.
results.evaluation: Claims C111-C112 accurately describe established PFT mechanisms based on multiple citations (Leung et al., Verma et al., Mondal and Chattopadhyay, De Schutter et al.). This provides appropriate context for highlighting the novelty of the CL mechanism.
